## What this chapter does

Use this chapter for ordinary **Quarto and website-content changes**.

Examples include:

- editing explanatory text;
- updating a briefing page after a new analytical package is published;
- adding or changing links and images;
- checking listings;
- checking the Downloads page; and
- changing site navigation.

The basic rule is simple:

> **Stata creates and controls the analytical products. Quarto presents them.**

Do not recalculate or manually correct surveillance results in a QMD file.

## Before you start

If the page uses new analytical results, confirm that the relevant Stata publication step has completed successfully first.

The approved files should already exist in the appropriate website mirror under `site/`.

Then:

1. start the local editing session using `start-info-hub-edit.bat`;
2. update local `main` and create a working branch as described in [Render and publish the website](render-publish.qmd); and
3. identify the QMD or website file that actually owns the content you need to change.

## Step 1: Open the source page in VS Code

Most public pages are under:

`site/`

Find the relevant `.qmd` file in the VS Code Explorer and open it.

Before editing:

- read the page heading and YAML header at the top;
- look for any maintenance note in the file; and
- check whether the page includes shared snippets or links to generated analytical files.

Do not edit anything under `site/_site/`. That folder is generated by Quarto.

## Step 2: Make the smallest necessary content change

For an ordinary page, edit the QMD directly.

Appropriate Quarto changes include:

- explanatory prose;
- headings;
- public methodological notes;
- links to approved resources;
- page metadata;
- images and captions; and
- layout or navigation where required.

Keep analytical numbers out of the QMD where an approved generated product already owns them.

If a public number or figure is wrong, stop. Return to the appropriate Stata workflow rather than correcting the rendered page by hand.

## Step 3: Save and check the local preview

Save the edited file.

The Quarto preview started by `start-info-hub-edit.bat` should normally refresh the browser automatically.

Check:

- spelling and headings;
- page layout;
- links;
- tables and figures;
- mobile/narrow-window readability where practical; and
- that the change says what you intended it to say.

Repeat the edit/preview cycle until the page is right.

## Step 4: Check links to analytical products

Website pages should link only to approved public resources.

For the BNR workflows, this normally means the relevant **website mirror** beneath `site/downloads/`.

Do not link a QMD directly to:

- `$BNR_STAGING`;
- `$BNR_PRIVATE`;
- a private review workbook;
- a confidential or deidentified analytical input; or
- an analyst's temporary local file.

See [The BNR analytics and publishing environment](../getting-started/environment.qmd) for the private/public folder model.

## Step 5: Run a full render and review

Before publishing the change, complete the full render described in [Chapter 10](render-publish.qmd).

Then inspect the affected page and any linked page it influences.

For example, a change to page metadata may also alter a Quarto listing; a change to `_quarto.yml` may alter navigation across the entire site.

## Maintain a surveillance dashboard

The CVD event and CVD mortality dashboards have dedicated maintenance pages because their Quarto/Observable controls must remain aligned with the approved public data structure.

- [Maintain the CVD events dashboard](cvd-events-dashboard.qmd)
- [Maintain the CVD mortality dashboard](cvd-mortality-dashboard.qmd)

The general rule remains that Quarto presents approved analytical products. The mortality dashboard year-to-date count is the one documented narrow presentation exception; its safeguards are defined on the mortality dashboard maintenance page. Do not extend that exception to other statistics without an explicit methods and architecture decision.

## Update an existing briefing

Routine briefing pages need several package-specific paths and narrative pieces to move together.

Use the dedicated How-To:

[Update an existing briefing](update-briefing.qmd)

That page covers:

- the new package ID;
- figures;
- workbook and ZIP links;
- shared narrative snippets;
- visible reporting-year text;
- PDF and slide links; and
- final listing checks.

Do not update the public briefing page until Briefing Step 3 has published the approved analytical package.

## Check the Downloads page

The central Downloads catalogue is built automatically before each Quarto render.

The builder reads the approved download records created by the publication workflows, including:

- briefing `downloads.yml` files;
- metric catalogue records; and
- tabulation `downloads.yml` files.

It then creates:

`site/downloads/downloads.yml`

### Normal operator rule

**Do not hand-edit the central `site/downloads/downloads.yml` file.**

Instead:

1. publish the analytical package through its Stata workflow;
2. confirm the package's own download record exists in the website mirror;
3. render the site; and
4. check the resulting Downloads page.

If the expected package does not appear, investigate the publication record or catalogue-builder error rather than adding a one-off manual entry.

## Check Quarto listings

Some Info-Hub pages use Quarto listings to collect and display other pages automatically.

For a routine listing update:

1. edit the source page and its metadata;
2. render the site;
3. open the listing page; and
4. check the title, date, description and ordering.

Do not edit the generated listing output under `site/_site/`.

If a listing itself needs a structural change, edit its source QMD or the relevant Quarto configuration and render the complete site afterwards.

## Change navigation or sidebars

Site-wide navigation is controlled mainly by:

`site/_quarto.yml`

Change this file carefully because one small YAML error can affect the whole website.

For a navigation change:

1. make only the required edit;
2. save `_quarto.yml`;
3. run a complete `quarto render`;
4. inspect the navbar and the affected sidebar; and
5. follow several neighbouring links before committing.

Do not edit `_quarto.yml` merely to solve a problem that belongs inside one page.

## Add an image or other public asset

Store ordinary public site images in the appropriate folder beneath:

`site/assets/`

Use relative links from the QMD where practical.

Before committing:

- confirm the image is suitable for public release;
- check its rendered size and caption;
- avoid unnecessarily large files; and
- check that the file appears in VS Code Source Control alongside the QMD that uses it.

Approved analytical figures should normally arrive through their controlled publication workflow rather than being copied manually into an arbitrary assets folder.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Useful website source locations

| Location | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `site/_quarto.yml` | Site-wide Quarto configuration, navigation and sidebars. |
| `site/assets/` | Public images, styles and other site assets. |
| `site/_shared/` | Shared snippets used by more than one page. |
| `site/downloads/` | Approved website-mirror downloads and the generated central catalogue. |
| `site/surveillance/` | Public surveillance pages, dashboards, tabulations and briefings. |
| `site/technical/` | Technical Manual source. |
| `site/operations/` | Operations Manual source. |
| `site/_site/` | Generated rendered website. Do not edit or commit. |
:::

## Step 6: Publish the website change

Once the local page and full render are satisfactory, return to [Render and publish the website](render-publish.qmd).

Use VS Code Source Control to:

1. inspect the changed files;
2. stage only the intended files;
3. commit them;
4. push the branch; and
5. merge the pull request into `main` when ready.

Then check GitHub Actions and the live site.

## Stop and return to Stata when...

Do not try to solve these problems in Quarto:

- an analytical value is wrong;
- a generated figure is wrong;
- suppression is wrong or incomplete;
- an analytical workbook contains the wrong data;
- a required public package is missing; or
- a website download points to an analytical package that was never approved and published.

Correct the problem through the appropriate analytical workflow, publish the new approved package, and then return to the Quarto page.
